intro: Teaching builds instructing, social perceptiveness and coordination skills, and all three are prized well beyond the classroom. Among the 25 careers below, the closest fit for former teachers is Instructional Coordinators, with an 81% skill match and BLS May 2025 median pay of $77,440.
why_it_works: Every school day you plan lessons, read a room full of different people and keep many moving parts on schedule. Those habits match what O*NET lists as most important in training, counseling and coordination roles. Trainers explain new systems to adults the way you explain fractions to kids. Counselors and social workers rely on the same patience and judgment you use with students and parents. The main gaps are business skills, such as operations analysis and managing a budget.
tips: Rewrite your resume in workplace terms: lesson planning becomes training design, and parent meetings become stakeholder communication.
Test a role before you switch: run a summer workshop, tutor adults or volunteer for your district's curriculum committee.
Check whether a target role needs a graduate degree before you apply, since 12 of the 25 matches usually do.

faq.q: What jobs can former teachers do?
faq.a: The closest matches by skills are Instructional Coordinators (81%), Training and Development Specialists (78%) and Child, Family, and School Social Workers (77%), based on O*NET 31.0 data. Training roles are the quickest move for many teachers, because 13 of the 25 matches need no more education than a teacher already has.

faq.q: Which careers for former teachers pay more?
faq.a: 8 of the 25 matches pay more than the $66,847 median for the teachers on this page. Instructional Coordinators earn a median of $77,440, which is 16% more, and Training and Development Specialists earn $69,280, or 4% more, according to BLS May 2025 data.

faq.q: Do former teachers need another degree to switch careers?
faq.a: Not always. 13 of the 25 matches usually need no extra education beyond a teaching background, including training, health education and recreational therapy roles. The other paths are steeper: 12 of the 25 usually need a graduate degree, such as instructional coordination and school counseling.

faq.q: What skills do teachers need to build for a new career?
faq.a: Across the top 10 matches, the skills that most often need work are operation and control, operations analysis, service orientation and managing financial resources. Your strongest skill, instructing, already rates 4.21 out of 5 in O*NET, so the gap is in business tasks rather than people skills.
